name: Child Sexual Abuse Directive (recast)
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: qualitative impact assessment; no quantified forecasts; not yet adopted
summary: The Commission expected the updated criminal-law rules to improve prevention, investigation and support for victims of child sexual abuse, but gave no figures. Its main monitoring tool is a new duty for countries to collect comparable statistics and survey victims every three years, which does not exist yet; a political agreement was reported in June 2026, so there is no evidence on effects.

indicators.objective: No LFS indicators; the memorandum relies on transposition checks, periodic Commission reports, and new obligations for Member States to collect statistics and run a population-based victim survey every 3 years (Eurostat methodology)

indicators.indicator: Administrative statistics on offences (Arts 3-9) and 3-yearly prevalence survey
indicators.target_or_baseline: Baseline cited in IA: at least one in five children falls victim to sexual violence
indicators.evidence: Not yet applicable: provisional agreement reported June 2026; not adopted or transposed. Current data not comparable across Member States.

indicators.indicator: Criminalise livestreamed abuse and online solicitation; longer limitation periods; national coordinating authorities
indicators.evidence: Benefits described qualitatively; costs to Member States described as limited and not quantified.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material (recast), SWD(2024) 33 (executive summary SWD(2024) 34)
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material (recast)
literature.headline: Qualitative benefits: better identification and support of victims, more effective prevention and investigation, reduced impunity for live-streamed abuse; costs mainly on Member State administrations, described as limited; no direct SME or competitiveness impact. Evaluation found that even with full transposition of the 2011 Directive, abuse is not adequately addressed
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the updated rules to help find and support more victims and prosecute more offenders, including for live-streamed abuse, at limited cost to national governments; it gave no numerical forecasts.
literature.verified: executive summary read; full text searched
